title: Rehearsal Is More Than Role Play
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Hughes argues that teacher rehearsal has become too narrowly equated with role play, when deliberate practice for teaching should look more like how musicians, athletes and surgeons train by isolating and repeating components of performance rather than always simulating the whole. She distinguishes routine expertise (fluent, automatic moves like giving instructions or explaining a concept) from adaptive expertise (responding to the unexpected), arguing rehearsal should build both. She introduces 'decision rehearsal' as a particularly valuable but underused form of practice, where teachers mentally rehearse responses to likely classroom scenarios before they occur. The piece closes by calling for a richer vocabulary of rehearsal types - verbal, decision, mental, fluency and interactive - matched to the specific skill being developed, rather than treating role play as the default answer.
points: Hughes's central reframe is that rehearsal should mean isolating and repeating components of teaching performance, not just simulating whole lessons through role play.
She argues adaptive expertise depends on routine expertise being automatic first, so rehearsal must build both fluency and responsiveness rather than treating them as competing priorities.
Her introduction of 'decision rehearsal' - mentally rehearsing responses to likely classroom scenarios in advance - offers a concrete, transferable technique distinct from role play.
She calls for a richer vocabulary of rehearsal types (verbal, decision, mental, fluency, interactive) matched to the specific skill, rather than a one-size-fits-all approach to practice.
quotes: Somewhere along the way, role play has become almost synonymous with rehearsal. The two are often used interchangeably, even though one is just a particular way of rehearsing.

Nobody expects a concert pianist to prepare by simply playing the whole piece over and over again. They isolate difficult passages. They slow them down. They practise finger patterns, dynamics and transitions before stitching everything back together.
The irony is that adaptive expertise depends on routine expertise. Teachers can only adapt effectively when the fundamentals no longer demand their attention.

What will you do if only three students understand the explanation? What if almost everyone gets the hinge question wrong? These aren't hypothetical distractions. They're the moments that define teaching. Rehearsing them develops professional judgement.

I wonder whether we also need a richer vocabulary. At the moment, rehearsal often means one thing. But perhaps we should be talking about verbal rehearsal, decision rehearsal, mental rehearsal, fluency rehearsal and interactive rehearsal.
